title: The Islamic Dilemma, answered
excerpt: What is the Islamic Dilemma? The argument, the verses it cites (5:47, 5:68, 10:94), the assumption it rests on, and the answer from the Qur’an and manuscripts.

title: The Islamic Dilemma without theology: the arguments answered
excerpt: The Islamic Dilemma restated without theology, its 2 steps and 4 exits answered point by point, and the dilemma it creates for the Christian.
body: The Islamic Dilemma has lately been restated in a form said to need no theology at all: anyone, believer or not, can run it. In this form it has 2 steps.

First, the Qur’an affirms that the Torah and the Injīl held by the Jews and Christians of the seventh century are inspired, preserved and authoritative. Second, the Qur’an contradicts doctrines that stand inside those books, above all the crucifixion, the divine sonship of Jesus and the manner of his miracles. A book that affirms and contradicts the same scripture cannot, it is concluded, come from an all-knowing God.

Four ways out are then offered and each is said to be unbearable for a Muslim: the Qur’an’s prophet stories are allegory; the Qur’an addresses some lost sect with its own books; the Qur’an’s author claimed to confirm what he did not confirm; or Christians of the fourth century held a salvific scripture that also taught what the Qur’an calls shirk.

A historically minded reply to this restatement has also been made, and it has been widely shared. It grants the first step outright and attacks the second with the tools of historical-critical scholarship: the Qur’an, it argues, alleges that interpretation was distorted and that the books were never lost, and nearly every supposed contradiction dissolves once the verses are read in the discourse of their own century. Much of that reply is sound and is used below. Part of it concedes more than the Qur’an says, and that part is set aside with reasons.
## The missing fifth exit

The 4 exits listed above share one assumption, which is the assumption the whole argument rests on: that the Injīl the Qur’an affirms is identical with the four gospels, so that affirming the one means endorsing every sentence of the other. The Qur’an does not say this, and the fifth exit, the Qur’an’s own, is the one the list leaves out.

The Injīl is what God gave to Jesus, “guidance and light” (5:46). The gospels are, on their own account, books written about him by others: Luke opens by saying that “many” had already drawn up accounts and that he used what was handed down (Luke 1:1-4).

The Qur’an calls itself muṣaddiq, confirming, and muhaymin, guardian, over the scripture before it (5:48), and a guardian keeps what is true and sets aside what is not. The revelation lies within the books, and the books hold more than the revelation. Every answer below returns to that distinction, which is set out in full on the Islamic Dilemma, answered and applied on the measure.
## The first step: what the Qur’an says is “with them”

The restated argument needs the first step in a strong form: the books in seventh-century hands are affirmed as preserved and authoritative, whole. The historical reply grants it. This website grants a weaker and more exact form, because that is what the verses say.

What the Qur’an plainly holds is that the Torah and the Injīl were present with the Jews and Christians it addressed. It tells them to bring the Torah and read it (3:93), and says the Prophet is “written with them in the Torah and the Injīl” (7:157).

It asks how they come to the Prophet for judgement “when they have the Torah, in which is God’s judgement” (5:43). They are accused of concealing the truth “while they know” (2:146; 3:71), and one can only conceal what one has.
On this point the historical reply is right and so are the argument’s proponents: the Qur’an does not say the earlier scripture was lost.
What the Qur’an never says is that the books in their hands were preserved whole and were authoritative in every line. It says the opposite in the same breath.

Some “write the book with their own hands and then say, This is from God” (2:79). Some “alter words from their places” (4:46; 5:13), “twist their tongues with the book so that you think it is from the book, and it is not from the book” (3:78), and “forgot a portion of what they were reminded of” (5:13-14). The People of the Book are told that the Prophet “makes clear to you much of what you used to hide of the book” (5:15).
A book of which “much” is hidden, and to which men have added pages of their own, is affirmed only as the place where the revelation is to be found, among other things.

The historical reply reads 2:79 well, and the reading supports this website’s position. The verse that follows quotes the people in question saying that the Fire will touch them only for a number of days (2:80), a rabbinic teaching (Mishnah ʿEduyot 2:10 gives the punishment of the wicked as 12 months). The charge is that human teaching was being passed off as the word of God.

The Christian writer Tertullian, in the third century, made the same complaint of the heretics of his day: “one man perverts the scriptures with his hand, another their meaning by his exposition” (De praescriptione haereticorum 38). Marcion cut the text with a knife; Valentinus kept the text and changed its sense. Tertullian thought the Bible mishandled, and still in the church’s hands. That is exactly the Qur’an’s complaint, and it is exactly what the gospels are: the sayings of Jesus, carried in books by men who shaped and added to them.
The synoptic problem shows the shaping being done, by the gospel writers themselves, within a generation.

So the first step is granted in this form only: the revelation given to Jesus was present with the Christians of the seventh century, carried in the books they read, which also carried what others had written. That is the Qur’an’s own position, and it is why there is no dilemma. The argument’s force depends entirely on the strong form, and the strong form is not in the text.
## The second step: the contradictions, one by one
### The crucifixion

All four gospels narrate the crucifixion, and the Qur’an says “they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them” (4:157). The argument counts this as a contradiction of an affirmed book. The Qur’an here measures the gospel writers’ report, and the measure is the point: a guardian over the record may say where the record is wrong.

The case for the Qur’an’s account, from the earliest Christian witnesses to a substitute onward, is on the end of his earthly mission and in section 26 of the gospel. The verse is treated point by point in The crucifixion and the Qur’an: six facts about 4:157 at Best of Islam.

The historical reply here goes a step too far in the other direction. It suggests that the early commentators show “nuance” on the crucifixion, as if some early opinion allowed that the Qur’an does not deny it, and that only Ibn Ḥazm in the eleventh century hardened the denial into dogma. The record does not bear that out.

What the early reports differ about is the identity of the substitute and whether Jesus tasted death before he was raised: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to read mutawaffīka in 3:55 as “causing you to die”, Wahb ibn Munabbih gives 3 hours of death, and Ibn Isḥāq reports that the Christians say 7 (al-Ṭabarī on 3:55); in each of these reports God then raises him. No early authority reports that the Jews crucified Jesus.

The denial was older than Ibn Ḥazm; he ruled on those who denied it. The commentaries themselves, translated in full, are on the classical commentaries, and the reader can test this against the texts themselves.
### Divine sonship, and why the Qur’an polices a word

The argument says the gospels teach that Jesus is the Son of God and the Qur’an denies it. The historical reply answers that “son of God” in the Hebrew Bible was the language of a king and his vassal, of Israel (Exodus 4:22), David (Psalm 2:7; 2 Samuel 7:14), the judges (Psalm 82:6) and the people (Hosea 11:1), and that Arabic walad means begotten offspring and nothing else, so the Qur’an refused the word because its hearers, pagan and Christian alike, took it as physical descent (6:101; 19:88-92; 43:57-58).

The second half of that is overstated: Arabic can use ibn figuratively, as the Qur’an itself does of the wayfarer, ibn al-sabīl (2:177). The first half is right and is enough. The gospels keep the old usage: the peacemakers “shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9), Adam is “the son of God” (Luke 3:38), and Jesus answers the charge of blasphemy by quoting Psalm 82, “I said, you are gods” (John 10:34-36).

The Qur’an denies what it names: that God “took a son” (ittakhadha waladan, 19:88-92), that He begets (112:3), that a man is to be worshipped as God (5:116-117). It leaves room for God to love His servants and choose them, and calls Abraham His friend (4:125).

What it refuses is a title that, in the mouths of the Christians it addressed, had come to mean a second divine person. On this it agrees with the gospels as the measure reads them, and the reading is set out on John and the Jesus who speaks of himself.
### “We are the children of God and His beloved” (5:18)

The argument treats 5:18 as a denial of a biblical doctrine, since the Torah calls Israel God’s children (Deuteronomy 14:1). The historical reply shows that the verse quotes a rabbinic saying almost word for word, “Beloved are Israel, for they are called children of God” (Mishnah Avot 3:14), and answers it with the Torah’s own conditional covenant: “they have dealt corruptly with Him; they are not His children” (Deuteronomy 32:5), “you are not My people” (Hosea 1:9).

That is correct, and the gospel says the same. When his hearers claim Abraham as their father, Jesus answers that if they were Abraham’s children they would do Abraham’s works, and that if God were their Father they would love him (John 8:39-42). John the Baptist tells them God can raise up children to Abraham from stones (Matthew 3:9).
The Qur’an’s question, “then why does He punish you for your sins?”, is the gospel’s own argument. There is no contradiction to find.
### Miracles “by God’s permission”

The argument finds a contradiction in the Qur’an’s repeated “by My permission” over the healings and the raising of the dead (3:49; 5:110), since Mark has Jesus heal and forgive without invoking any authority, and the scribes call it blasphemy (Mark 2:5-7). But the gospels themselves supply the permission.

Matthew, retelling the same scene, ends it with the crowd glorifying God “who had given such authority to men” (Matthew 9:8). Jesus looks up to heaven and sighs before he heals (Mark 7:34), thanks the Father before he calls Lazarus (John 11:41-42), says he can do nothing of himself (John 5:30) and that “the Father who dwells in me does the works” (John 14:10), and casts out devils “by the finger of God” (Luke 11:20).

Peter’s first sermon calls him “a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs which God did through him” (Acts 2:22), and Peter again: “God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power; he went about doing good and healing, for God was with him” (Acts 10:38). The Qur’an’s phrase is Peter’s.

The historical reply adds that the Qur’an is answering 2 audiences at once, the Jewish charge that the signs were sorcery (compare 5:110, “those who disbelieved among them said, This is nothing but plain magic”, and 61:6) and the Christian inference that they made him God. That is the measure at work: the signs are kept, and both false readings of them are set aside.
### The “I am” sayings of John

The argument rests its weight at last on John: “I and the Father are one” (10:30), “my Lord and my God” (20:28), and the prologue’s Word that “was God”. The historical reply, following a Muslim academic, gives a Sunni reading of each: unity of will and commission rather than of essence, as the Qur’an says “whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God” (4:80) and “you did not throw when you threw, but God threw” (8:17); the vocative of surprise in Thomas’s cry; the Word as God’s creative and revelatory agent, as the rabbis read it.
Some of this is defensible. This website does not need it, because the measure is there to sort the material, and sorting leaves some of John outside the revelation.

John is the latest of the four and the one in which Jesus speaks of himself in a voice the other three do not know. Where John has him say what the others do not, and what the Qur’an sets aside, the measure marks it as beyond the revelation, and the reasons are given on the John page.

The measure keeps a great deal of John, and the Qur’an echoes much of it: “the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent” (17:3), “the Father is greater than I” (14:28), “I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (20:17), which the Qur’an gives back as “God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him” (3:51; 19:36; 43:64).

The argument’s proponents say the author of John meant to equate Jesus with God and that no charitable reading can avoid it. If so, the author of John is one of the men whose hands the Qur’an describes, and the dilemma has no second horn.
### “The Injīl commands offensive war” (9:111)

The argument says 9:111 attributes to the Torah and the Injīl a promise that those who fight and are slain in God’s way have Paradise, and that no gospel says any such thing; a human author, not knowing the canon, could make that slip. The historical reply points out that the verse speaks of a promise: God has bought the believers’ lives for Paradise, “a true promise binding upon Him in the Torah and the Injīl and the Qur’an”.

The promise that the one who gives his life for God receives life is in all 3 books. The Torah has Israel fight at God’s command with God fighting for them (Deuteronomy 20:1-4) and the psalmist say “for Your sake we are killed all the day long” (Psalm 44:22), which Paul of Tarsus quotes of the martyrs (Romans 8:36).

The gospel has “whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel’s will save it” (Mark 8:35), “blessed are those persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:10-12), “today you will be with me in Paradise” to the man dying beside him (Luke 23:43), and “be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation 2:10). Christians read these as the charter of martyrdom for 6 centuries before the Qur’an.
The verse says the bargain is old, and it is.
### “This is in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses” (87:19)

The argument says 87:18-19 places the Qur’an’s descriptions of the Garden and the Fire in the scripture of Moses, where they are not. But the “this” of verse 18 is what the preceding verses say: he prospers who purifies himself and remembers his Lord’s name and prays, “but you prefer the life of this world, and the Hereafter is better and more lasting” (87:14-17).

That is the teaching of Deuteronomy 30:19-20, “choose life”, of Moses’ lament that his people would not “consider their latter end” (Deuteronomy 32:29), and of the one psalm the Bible ascribes to Moses, “teach us to number our days” (Psalm 90:12).
The scrolls of Abraham the Bible does not contain; Jewish and Christian antiquity knew several books under his name. The verse says nothing about the furniture of Paradise.
### “The Qur’an says Jesus was literate”

The restatement claims, from 3:48 and 5:110, that the Qur’an says Jesus was taught to write, and builds on it. The classical commentators read it the same way: al-Ṭabarī, al-Jalālayn, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī (from Ibn Jurayj) and Ibn Kathīr all gloss al-kitāb in these verses as writing. The verses say God taught him “the Book and the Wisdom and the Torah and the Injīl”, so the scripture taught to Jesus is named apart, as the Torah and the Injīl.

What the argument builds on the word does not follow from it. That Jesus could write says nothing about who wrote the four gospels, or that any of them is the Injīl the same verse says God taught him.
### “The Qur’an does not know the canon”

The argument says the Qur’an shows it does not know what the Injīl contains, since it recounts the clay birds and the speech from the cradle, which are in no gospel, and speaks of “the Injīl” in the singular. Two answers.

The Qur’an recounts the clay birds and the cradle as God’s favours to Jesus (5:110) and never places them in the Injīl, and the Christians of the Near East told those very stories, which stand in the Infancy Gospel of Thomas and the Arabic Infancy Gospel. What the Qur’an says is in the Injīl it names: guidance, light and admonition (5:46), the description of the Prophet (7:157), the likeness of the believers as a growing crop (48:29), and the promise of 9:111.

The singular is the Christians’ own usage, “the Gospel according to”, one gospel in 4 tellings, and the gospel in widest use in Syriac was Tatian’s harmony, a single book. On this the historical reply and the argument’s proponents agree, and so does this website; the singular shows the Qur’an’s knowledge of its audience.
### The Prophet “written with them”

The argument sets a higher bar for the Qur’an than for the New Testament: the Qur’an says Jews and Christians “know him as they know their sons” (2:146; 6:20) and that he is “written with them” (7:157), so the description must be plain and the communities must have been convinced, whereas Matthew has only typology. The same verse says a party of them “conceal the truth while they know” (2:146), so the communities were not all convinced. The claim is that the learned recognised the description and that some hid it, which is a claim about what they knew.

The texts Muslims have always read this way are on the good news of Aḥmad: the prophet like Moses from among their brethren (Deuteronomy 18:18), the one who comes from Paran (Deuteronomy 33:2; Habakkuk 3:3), the servant in whom Kedar and Sela rejoice (Isaiah 42:1-11), and the Counsellor who will not speak of himself (John 16:13).
Whether those texts persuade is a fair question. The double standard is the unfair part, and the next section turns to it.
### Christians of the fourth century

The last exit offered is said to be the hardest: on the Qur’an’s terms Christians 3 centuries before the Prophet held a scripture that could save them and that also taught shirk. The Qur’an has an answer and gives it.

It says of those who believed in God and the Last Day and did right among the Jews, Christians and Sabians that they have their reward (2:62; 5:69), that among the People of the Book is “an upright community who recite God’s verses in the night” (3:113-115), that God gave “those of them who believed their reward” while “many of them are transgressors” (57:27), that the followers of Jesus fell into sects (19:37; 43:65), and that God does not punish until He has sent a messenger (17:15).

A Christian of the fourth century who followed the guidance in his gospel was on the path; one who built on the additions was judged by what he knew. That is the position of every tradition that believes God spoke before it did.
## Confirming, the Book and the law
The historical reply does its best work on the verbs.

Muṣaddiq, confirming, in 5:44-48 and 3:50, is used of Jesus confirming the Torah while making lawful part of what had been forbidden, which is the claim of the Sermon on the Mount, “I came not to abolish but to fulfil” (Matthew 5:17), and of the Didascalia Apostolorum, a church order read across the Syriac world, which taught that Christ confirmed the law and lifted the “second legislation” laid on Israel after the calf.

In 5:45 the Qur’an cites the law of retaliation from Exodus 21:23-25, insists on it against the rabbinic practice of commuting it to money (Mishnah Bava Qamma 8:1), and then opens the door that Matthew 5:38-39 opens: whoever forgoes it as charity, it is an expiation for him. The Qur’an is arbitrating between the Torah’s letter and the gospel’s mercy and binding both.

Muhaymin in 5:48, guardian or arbiter, sits in a verse whose verb is “judge”, so the debate over the word changes little; a guardian who judges is an arbiter, and both readings are given on the measure.

And al-kitāb, when the Qur’an says it confirms “the Book” before it, most often means the Torah, the scripture of law and history; the Injīl is paired instead with “the Wisdom” (5:110), and the jinn who hear the Qur’an call it “a Book sent down after Moses, confirming what was before it” (46:30), naming Moses as the scripture it follows. All of this strengthens the pillar page’s second answer: to confirm is to confirm the revelation, in the first place its law and its account of God.
## Where this website parts from the historical reply

- The first step is granted only in its weaker form. The Qur’an affirms that the revelation was present with the People of the Book, and it names the kinds of alteration it has in mind in their books, of meaning (3:78; 4:46) and of text (2:79). This website uses either charge only where it can be shown from the texts, as the measure sets out.

- The Injīl is identified with neither the four gospels nor Tatian’s harmony. The gospels carry the Injīl and carry other things. The historical reply, having said that the Qur’an “is Matthew, Mark, Luke and John” in paraphrase, has no way left to say where the Qur’an and John part company except to reinterpret John, and that is the trap the argument sets.

- The early Muslim commentators were undecided about the substitute and about whether Jesus died before being raised, and agreed that he was not crucified. The translated commentaries are on the site for anyone to check.

- The answer rests on no single school. The reply notes that literalist readers are a minority among Muslims and that Sufi and Shia traditions carry a higher prophetology able to absorb John’s language. That may be so. The measure used here needs none of it: the Qur’an as it reads, and the gospels as they read, are enough.

- The reply ends by saying that no polemic can prove a scripture false and that each side should stop. This website makes a narrower claim and stands by it: the gospels, read by their own evidence, are layered books by several hands, and the Qur’an is the measure over them. That is a claim about texts and it can be checked.
## The biblical dilemma

The argument asks the Qur’an for a standard of agreement with the earlier scripture that its own proponents could not survive. If “confirm” must mean that every doctrine of the New Testament stands written in the Old, then the New Testament fails first, and by a wider margin.

Isaiah 7:14, read by Matthew of the virgin birth (Matthew 1:22-23), is in its own context a sign to King Ahaz about a young woman (ʿalmāh) and a child to be born within a few years, before the Assyrian threat passed. Hosea 11:1, “out of Egypt I called My son”, which Matthew applies to the flight to Egypt (Matthew 2:15), names Israel as the son and the Exodus as the calling.

The servant of Isaiah 53 is named as Israel in the surrounding chapters (Isaiah 41:8; 44:1; 49:3). Matthew says the prophets wrote “he shall be called a Nazarene” (Matthew 2:23) and no prophet did. Matthew reads Zechariah’s one animal as a pair (Matthew 21:5-7) and credits Jeremiah with Zechariah’s thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 27:9).

No text of the Hebrew Bible names a Messiah called Jesus. The historical reply is right to note that Gabriel Said Reynolds, no Muslim, has written that the Qur’an stands closer to the New Testament than the New Testament stands to the Hebrew Bible.

Christian apologists meet all this with typology: the earlier text foreshadows the later, and the later reveals what the earlier meant. That is a legitimate way to read scripture. It is also exactly the way the Qur’an reads the earlier scripture, retelling its stories, as the historical reply puts it, as a homily or a targum does, assuming the hearer knows why Sarah laughed (11:71) and why the priests cast lots for Mary (3:44), varying the detail (the beast that took Joseph is a wolf, 12:17) and drawing out the meaning.

The Qur’an calls itself “a detailed exposition of the Book” (tafṣīl al-kitāb, 10:37). The apologist who allows typology to Matthew and forbids it to the Qur’an, who rejects every text Muslims read of Muhammad by historical context and reads Isaiah 7:14 of Jesus by faith, is using 2 measures.

Whichever measure he keeps, he loses the argument: with the strict one the New Testament falls before the Qur’an is reached; with the generous one the Qur’an’s confirmation of the earlier scripture is no more strained than Matthew’s. And a Christian who presses the strict measure against the Qur’an in public has handed the secular critic the knife and shown him where to cut.
That is why the historical reply calls it a dilemma for the Christian.
## What the restated argument gets right

Fairness requires the list. The Qur’an does engage the gospels in their sixth- and seventh-century forms, including the infancy traditions and Tatian’s harmony, because those were the forms its hearers knew; this website says so on how this gospel was composed.

The Qur’an does disagree with the gospel writers on the crucifixion and with John on the person of Jesus, and no reading of the verbs makes those disagreements go away; this website explains them. And the question the argument asks, what the Injīl is and where it is, is the right question. The answer is the one the Qur’an gives and the gospels illustrate: a revelation given to a man, carried by other men in books that bear their marks.
## Questions about the argument in this form
? Can the Islamic Dilemma be argued without theology?

It can be stated without theology, and it fails without theology, because its first step misreports the Qur’an. The Qur’an says the earlier revelation is present with the People of the Book and that their books also contain what men wrote and misread (2:79; 3:78; 5:15). No faith is needed to see that the strong form of the first step is not in the text.
? Does Qur’an 9:111 say the Gospel commands war?

No. It says a promise is found in the Torah, the Injīl and the Qur’an: that the one who gives his life in God’s way has Paradise. Mark 8:35, Matthew 5:10-12, Luke 23:43 and Revelation 2:10 state that promise, and Christians had read them as the charter of martyrdom for 6 centuries.
? Does the Qur’an contradict the gospels on how Jesus worked miracles?

No. The Qur’an says he healed and raised the dead “by God’s permission” (3:49; 5:110). Matthew says the crowd glorified God “who had given such authority to men” (9:8), John has Jesus thank the Father before raising Lazarus (11:41-42), and Peter calls him “a man attested by God with wonders which God did through him” (Acts 2:22).
? Does Qur’an 5:18 deny what the Torah says about Israel?

No. It quotes the rabbinic saying that Israel is beloved as God’s children (Mishnah Avot 3:14) and answers it as Deuteronomy 32:5, Hosea 1:9, Matthew 3:9 and John 8:39-42 answer it: the relationship is conditional on obedience.
? Did early Muslim scholars accept that Jesus was crucified?

No. They differed about who was made to resemble him and about whether he died before being raised, and all of them held that the one crucified was another. The claim that Ibn Ḥazm invented the denial reverses the record. The commentaries are translated in full on the classical commentaries.
? Does the Qur’an say Jesus was taught to write?

No. It says God taught him “the Book and the Wisdom” (3:48; 5:110), the fixed phrase for a prophet’s instruction in scripture (2:129; 62:2). The classical commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Jalālayn, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr) read the Book here as writing, so yes; but the same verse names the scripture he was taught as the Torah and the Injīl, and his writing says nothing about who wrote the four gospels.

title: Pfander’s Balance of Truth: the Christian polemic at its source
excerpt: Pfander’s Mīzān al-Ḥaqq (1829; English 1866), the source of the Christian case against the Qur’an on the earlier scriptures, answered chapter by chapter.
body: The Islamic Dilemma was argued before it had a name. Karl Gottlieb Pfander (1803 to 1865), a Basel missionary who worked in the Caucasus, in India and at Constantinople, wrote Mīzān al-Ḥaqq, The Balance of Truth, in German at Shusha in 1829, had it printed in Armenian in 1831 and in Persian in 1835, and carried it into Urdu, Arabic and Turkish.

R. H. Weakley’s English translation appeared in London in 1866, and W. St Clair Tisdall revised the book in 1910. For a century it was the handbook of Christian controversy with Muslims, and the argument this website answers is its argument.

The book argues for far more than the question at issue here: its second part sets out Christian doctrine and its third attacks the Prophet and the Qur’an. The first part is the one that matters for the Injīl, and it is answered below.
The text used is Weakley’s translation of 1866, from the Bodleian Library copy digitised by Google; the quotations are short and have been checked against the scan.
## What Pfander argued

The first part of the book has 3 chapters, and their titles are the argument. The books current among Christians, “i.e. the Old and New Testaments”, are “declared by the Koran to be Divine revelations”. Those books were “never at any time abrogated”. And the Muslim assertion that they “have been corrupted and changed” is “refuted”.

The first chapter cites 5 verses (42:15; 29:46; 5:5; 2:44; 3:3) to show that the Qur’an honours the scriptures of the People of the Book, then adds in a sentence what the whole case needs: “It is also evident that the books understood to have been given to the Jews and Christians are the Old and New Testaments.” The conclusion follows at once: “whosoever accepts the Koran must accept them.”

The third chapter asks the questions that later apologists have repeated: “at what period, by whom, and in what manner this tampering with the text was effected; and which are the corrupted passages”. It argues that Christians had no motive to corrupt their books and no means, since they were scattered from Spain to India and divided among themselves; that the great codices in Rome, St Petersburg, London and Paris, and the quotations of the Fathers, agree with the printed Bibles; that the Qur’an itself sends the Prophet to “those who have read the book before thee” (10:94; 21:7); and that Jesus never charged the Jews with corrupting the Torah.

Then comes the turn that the Islamic Dilemma later made its whole case. Pfander writes that the Prophet “acknowledged the Old and New Testaments to be the Word of God; and on the other, he taught a religion at variance with those books; and so, to cover this discrepancy, he was obliged to assert that they had been corrupted.” That is the dilemma of 1829: affirm the books and contradict them, or call them corrupt and lose the affirmation.
## Where the argument meets this website
### “The books given to the Jews and Christians are the Old and New Testaments”

Pfander asserts the identification in one sentence and never argues it. The Qur’an speaks of one Injīl, given to ʿĪsā as the Torah was given to Mūsā (5:46), and every use of the word is singular. The four gospels are, on their own account, books written about him by others; Luke opens his by saying that many had already drawn up accounts and that he used what was handed down (Luke 1:1-4).

The Christians Pfander wrote for in Persia and India read a Bible that the Christians of the Qur’an’s own century did not possess in that form: the Syriac churches read Tatian’s harmony of the four gospels, and their New Testament had 22 books. The first answer on the Islamic Dilemma, answered sets this out, and the five gospels show what the books are.
### “Whosoever accepts the Koran must accept them”

The verse Pfander does not quote is 5:48, where the Qur’an calls itself muṣaddiq, confirming, and muhaymin, guardian, over the scripture before it. Al-Ṭabarī reads the guardian as the trustworthy custodian: what in the earlier books agrees with the Qur’an is true, and what disagrees with it is false.

Confirming a revelation and certifying every line of the books that carry it are different acts, and the same verse that has Jesus confirm the Torah has him make lawful part of what it forbade (3:50). Pfander’s own second chapter grants the principle when it says that the Gospel did not abrogate the Torah but “completed what had been begun”; the Qur’an says the same of itself, and adds the word guardian. The measure applies it.
### “Not a single passage … more precise than the general statement”

Pfander says the Qur’an never specifies what was corrupted. It names the kinds. Some “write the book with their own hands and then say, This is from God” (2:79); others “alter words from their places” (4:46; 5:13) or “twist their tongues with the book” so that it is taken for scripture (3:78); and some conceal much of it (5:15).
Alteration of the text and alteration of its meaning are both charged, and this website charges each only where it can be shown.

Pfander also dates the corruption from Sūrat al-Bayyina (98:4) to the years after the Prophet appeared; but the verse speaks of the People of the Book dividing among themselves, tafarraqa, and says nothing about their text. The third answer on the pillar page gives the verses in full.
### “At what period, by whom, and in what manner”

The question assumes a conspiracy, and this website needs none. The gospels were layered when they were written: Mark first, Matthew and Luke rewriting Mark with other material, John last and apart. That is the finding of the scholarship of the 2 centuries since Pfander, and it is set out on the synoptic problem.
The additions that textual criticism has since identified were made by copyists in the first centuries, long before Islam, and no Christian in the seventh century had a motive to make them.

Pfander’s own witnesses tell against him here. He names the Codex Vaticanus and the codex then in St Petersburg, now the Codex Sinaiticus, as agreeing with the printed Bibles. Both end Mark at 16:8, without the appearances and the ascension that the printed Bibles of his day carried; both omit the woman taken in adultery (John 7:53 to 8:11); neither has the heavenly witnesses of 1 John 5:7.
He could not know this in 1829, when neither codex had been published. The reader of 1866 could, and the reader of today can see it on the page on Mark and the discrepancy tables.
### “Christ never charged the Jews with corrupting the Torah”

Jesus is recorded saying that the Jews had made the word of God void by their tradition (Mark 7:13), and that “Moses, for the hardness of your hearts, wrote you this precept” (Mark 10:5). The gospels’ Jesus distinguishes the commandment of God from what had been written and taught beside it. That is the Qur’an’s distinction too, and it is the whole of this website’s position: the revelation lies within the books, and the Qur’an is the measure that sorts it from the rest.
### The collection of the Qur’an

Pfander turns the charge round and argues from the reports of the readings and of ʿUthmān’s codex that the Qur’an itself might be corrupt. The question is outside this website, which answers the Christian case about the Injīl and does not pursue the Christian case against the Qur’an. One remark belongs here.

The reports Pfander quotes are in Bukhārī, where every Muslim can read them; the tradition that records the history of its own text in its canonical collections is doing the opposite of concealing it. The manuscripts and the reports are set out at Best of Islam: ʿUthmān’s copies and manuscript transmission in the Qur’an and the New Testament.
### The Prophet foretold

The first chapter of Pfander’s third part is the ancestor of the standard Christian reply on Aḥmad: the name is not in the Gospel, the Paraclete of John 14 to 16 is the Holy Spirit, and the Qur’an’s claim came from “some apostate Christian” who flattered the Prophet. The last is a guess, offered without a source. The rest is answered, and its force conceded where it has force, on the good news of Aḥmad. Pfander’s footnote on the word ummī, which he renders “illiterate”, is answered in Was Muḥammad illiterate? at Best of Islam.
## What Pfander has right
Three of his points stand. The Gospel did not abrogate the Torah; Matthew 5:17 says so, and the Qur’an says that Jesus confirmed what was before him (3:50; 61:6).

The Qur’an does send its hearers to the People of the Book (10:94; 16:43; 21:7), and this website reads those verses as it reads 7:157: the revelation was present with them, carried in the books they held. And no Christian in the seventh century replaced the gospels; the manuscripts show that the text of the four has been copied with care since the fourth century, and this website says so.

None of this reaches the conclusion. A book carried faithfully for 12 centuries is still a book about Jesus, written by others, and the question of what in it is the Injīl given to him is the question Pfander never asked.
## From Pfander to the Islamic Dilemma

Raḥmatullāh al-Kairānawī answered the book in its own day: he debated Pfander at Agra in April 1854 and published Iẕhār al-Ḥaqq, The Demonstration of Truth, at Constantinople in 1864, using the European biblical criticism of his time against the claim that the text had never changed. Pfander’s book was revised in 1910 and reprinted through the twentieth century, and the two-horned form that Answering Islam and Acts 17 Apologetics gave the argument in the 2000s and 2010s is Pfander’s sentence about the Prophet being “obliged to assert that they had been corrupted”, turned into a dilemma and pressed on video. The pillar page follows the line from Celsus and Julian, through the apology under the name of al-Kindī and Isṭifān Ward, to Pfander and his successors.
## Questions about Pfander and the Balance of Truth
? Who was Karl Gottlieb Pfander?

A German missionary of the Basel Mission (1803 to 1865) who worked at Shusha in the Caucasus, then in India for the Church Missionary Society, then at Constantinople. He wrote Mīzān al-Ḥaqq in 1829 and debated Raḥmatullāh al-Kairānawī at Agra in 1854.
? What does the Balance of Truth argue?

That the Qur’an declares the Old and New Testaments to be the word of God, that they were never abrogated or corrupted, and that the Prophet was therefore obliged to call them corrupt because his teaching differed from them. Its second part sets out Christian doctrine and its third attacks the Qur’an and the Prophet.
? Did Muslims answer it?

Yes, from the first. Raḥmatullāh al-Kairānawī’s Iẕhār al-Ḥaqq (1864) was written against it after the Agra debate of 1854, and it remains in print. Avril Powell’s Muslims and Missionaries in Pre-Mutiny India gives the history of the controversy.
? Is the Islamic Dilemma in Pfander?

In substance. The name and the two-horned form came later. His sentence that the Prophet acknowledged the books as the word of God and taught against them, and so had to call them corrupt, is the dilemma in one line. The modern form adds nothing to his premises, and it fails where his fail: the Injīl is taken to be the four gospels, and confirming is taken to mean certifying every word.
